meta.reportLabel: Thu - TWO CORRECTIONS AND A BREAK. First, THE YEN THESIS WAS WRONG YESTERDAY AND IS FIXED TODAY: June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% y/y IN LINE with consensus, base pay accelerated to 3.4% from 3.0%, real wages gained 1.6% for a sixth straight month and nominal wages have now run above 3% for five months, the longest streak in 34 years. The BoJ's monetary leg is intact, not dead - JPY is upgraded from 0 to +1 and USD/JPY goes back to SHORT. Second, THE DOLLAR BROKE: ADP added just 44k against 70k expected, the weakest in six months, and ISM services printed 54.1 against 54.5 with the EMPLOYMENT INDEX AT 47.4 in outright contraction. Two labour misses in two days after JOLTS at 7.14m. The September hike is effectively priced out and USD drops to -1. Third, METALS EXPLODED ON THE PEACE TRADE: gold jumped 3.8% to about $4,231, its biggest single day since February, and silver surged 5.1% to $62.59, because a Hormuz reopening cuts the inflation path and therefore the Fed - the metals are trading US real rates, not the war. A 60-day interim deal is drafted and awaiting the final Iranian sign-off. WTI $74.79. Cleanest trades: EUR/USD LONG, XAU LONG, XAG LONG, EUR/NZD LONG, NZD/JPY SHORT. meta.regime: Two of yesterday's calls have to be corrected on the data, and both corrections point the same way - against the dollar. The larger of the two is the yen. Japan's June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% y/y, matching the Bloomberg median rather than missing it; contractual earnings also rose 3.4% with full-time employees at 3.6%; base pay accelerated to 3.4% from 3.0% in May; special payments jumped 10.3%; and real wages rose 1.6% for a sixth consecutive monthly gain. Nominal wage growth has now exceeded 3% for five straight months, the longest such run in 34 years. That is the wage-price cycle the Bank of Japan said it needed, and it sits alongside Tokyo July core CPI at 1.9% from 1.6% and Tokyo ex-food-and-energy at 2.0%. The yen therefore has a monetary engine underneath the joint MoF and US Treasury bid, not just a level defence, and it goes from 0 back to +1. The second correction is the dollar, and here the market did the work: ADP private payrolls rose only 44,000 in July against 70,000 expected and 95,000 in June, the weakest in six months, and the ISM services index came in at 54.1 against 54.5 with the employment sub-index collapsing to 47.4 from 51.2 expected, into outright contraction, even as prices paid stayed elevated at 70.3. That is now three consecutive soft labour reads - JOLTS openings at 7.14 million from 7.50 million, ADP, and the ISM services employment component - against a July FOMC where three members dissented FOR a hike. DXY sits at 99.84. The third leg is the metals, and it is the cleanest expression of the whole regime: gold rose 3.8% to roughly $4,231, its biggest daily gain since February, and silver 5.1% to $62.59, both RISING on Hormuz de-escalation because a reopening lowers the inflation path and therefore the Fed path. Falling real rates beat the disappearing war premium. The euro remains top of the board on July HICP at 2.9% with core at 2.5% and a final composite PMI revised up to 52.0.

dailyRead: Sell the dollar and own the metals. The two data points that landed yesterday both cut the same way: ADP private payrolls at +44k against +70k expected was the weakest in six months, and the ISM services employment index fell to 47.4 from an expected 51.2, into contraction, while the headline only managed 54.1 against 54.5. Stack those on Tuesday's JOLTS at 7.14 million from 7.50 million and the three July FOMC dissenters have lost their labour market. DXY is at 99.84 and the September hike is effectively out of the price, so USD drops from 0 to -1 and EUR/USD becomes a directional LONG rather than a range - the three-point score gap is now the widest dollar setup on the board. The second and more important change is a correction to yesterday's yen call, which was built on a wage print that did not happen. Japan's June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% y/y, in line with the Bloomberg median, contractual earnings also 3.4% with full-timers at 3.6%, base pay accelerating to 3.4% from 3.0%, and real wages up 1.6% for a sixth straight month - the fifth consecutive month of nominal growth above 3%, the longest streak in 34 years. That is precisely the sustained wage-price cycle the Bank of Japan has conditioned its next hike on, and with Tokyo July core CPI at 1.9% from 1.6% and Tokyo ex-food-and-energy at 2.0%, the October window is live again. The yen goes back to +1, USD/JPY returns to SHORT MEDIUM, JPYBASKET to LONG, and NZD/JPY at a three-point gap becomes the best carry-unwind ticket on the board. Third, the metals: gold jumped 3.8% to about $4,231, its largest single-session gain since February, and silver 5.1% to $62.59, and both did it INTO Hormuz de-escalation headlines - because a reopening lowers the inflation path, which lowers the Fed path, which lowers real rates. That transmission beats the loss of the war premium, and it makes XAU/USD and XAG/USD the two highest-conviction longs today rather than the low-medium tickets they were yesterday. Silver additionally has the industrial leg with the DAX at a record 26,202. On the geopolitics itself, the deal is now a 60-day interim arrangement: ships entering the Gulf via an Iranian-controlled route, exiting through Omani waters, no transit fees, contingent on the US lifting its naval blockade, with the draft finalised and Iranian sign-off reportedly completed Tuesday. Trump said it could be announced any day. WTI is $74.79 and USOIL stays RANGE - the structural short has already paid, the announcement is a two-way event from here, and the curve is still backwardated. The euro keeps the top spot on core HICP at 2.5% and a composite PMI revised up to 52.0, but the counterargument arrived with producer prices decelerating to 4.6% from 5.9%. New Zealand stays the short leg at -2 after a 5.6% unemployment print, though note that July business confidence jumped to 56.1 from 36.6 and the manufacturing PMI hit 59.7 - the kiwi is broken on rates, not on activity, so run the crosses rather than the outright. Australia's June trade balance swung to a AUD 1,929m surplus from a 2,367m deficit, a far better outcome than the consensus deficit, which supports AUD into the RBA on Aug 11.

USD.when: Sept 16 FOMC (hike now effectively priced out)
USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. That hawkish case has now been dismantled by the labour data in three sessions: JOLTS job openings fell to 7.14m from 7.50m, ADP added just 44k in July against 70k expected and 95k in June, and the ISM services employment index dropped to 47.4 from an expected 51.2, into contraction. The headline ISM services still printed 54.1 with prices paid at 70.3, and July ISM manufacturing was 55.6, so the growth side is not broken - the hiring side is. June CPI 3.5%, core 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5%, payrolls +57k, unemployment 4.2%. July jobs on Aug 7 and July CPI on Aug 12 are what remain.

EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike (refi 2.40%, MLF 2.65%), confirmed unchanged Jul 23. July flash HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4%, services inflation 3.3% and energy inflation 10%. Growth turned too - Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y after a flat Q1, with the FINAL July composite PMI revised up to 52.0, services 51.7 from 49.4 and manufacturing 51.9. Wage growth 3.4%, negotiated wages 2.46%, unemployment 6.3%. The single counterargument is pipeline: producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y from 5.9%, which says the 10% energy-inflation print unwinds mechanically once $75 crude feeds through in the autumn.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. June CPI 2.6%, core 2.6%, services 3.6%. The labour market is firmer than the pause implies - employment +148k in May, wages 4.3%, unemployment 4.9% - and July services PMI jumped to 51.8 from 48.8 with the composite at 52.1. The soft spots are the claimant count rising 6.7k and manufacturing revised down to 51.9. TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%. No domestic data this week, so sterling is a follower.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (Oct is now the live window)
JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. THE WAGE LEG IS INTACT - this is a correction to yesterday's read. June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% y/y, matching the Bloomberg median; contractual cash earnings also 3.4% with full-time employees at 3.6% and part-timers 2.9%; base pay accelerated to 3.4% from 3.0% in May; special payments +10.3%; and real wages rose 1.6% for a sixth consecutive month. Nominal growth has exceeded 3% for five straight months, the longest streak in 34 years. Add Tokyo July core CPI at 1.9% from 1.6% and Tokyo ex-food-and-energy at 2.0%. The July Outlook Report's cut to FY2026 CPI of 2.5% from 2.8% is the offset, but October is live again, and the joint MoF and US Treasury operation now sits on top of a real rates story rather than substituting for one.

AUD.note: Cash rate 4.35% after three hikes in 2026 (Feb, Mar, May) on the energy shock. Q2 trimmed mean 3.6% but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%, which is not a pause profile. June trade swung to a AUD 1,929m surplus from a 2,367m deficit, though terms of trade slipped to 112 from 117. July services PMI revised up to 53.6 and composite 53.2, unemployment 4.4% with employment +76.3k. Against all that, consumer inflation expectations dropped hard to 4.7% from 5.5% and cheaper crude pulls Q3 CPI down. TE's model still carries 4.60%; the market expects no change.

NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years. That cycle is finished. Q2 unemployment printed 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since Q3 2015; underutilisation widened to 13.8%; and the labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y. Employment rose 0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%. The Q2 CPI of 4.1% that triggered July's move was 27.5% petrol, and crude is down roughly 13% in three sessions. The genuine offset is sentiment: July business confidence jumped to 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ consumer confidence to 99.3 from 91.3 and the manufacturing PMI to 59.7. Two-year inflation expectations 2.53%.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting. June CPI cooled to 2.8% with CPI-trim and CPI-median BOTH BELOW target as gasoline decelerated sharply. Q1 GDP 0.0% q/q and -0.1% y/y, unemployment 6.6% after a +87.8k employment rebound, wage growth 3.5%. There is no rates leg at all, so the loonie is a pure terms-of-trade trade with WTI at $74.79 - and its terms of trade are being negotiated in Muscat rather than set in Ottawa. The July jobs report lands tomorrow alongside the US print.

CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held Dec, Mar and Jun; panellists see no change until 2027. July CPI came in at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected, down from 0.5%, with core unchanged at 0.3% - under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast, and Nomura now models Q3 at 0.5%. Domestic prices rose 0.5% while imported prices were flat as energy cost pressure eased. Producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y and unemployment is 2.9%. FX reserves rose to CHF 758.8bn in June. The June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only; the SNB is content to let the franc slide.

symbols.why: Three-point gap. Both currencies were levered to oil in opposite directions and the euro has broken that link - its hike pricing now rests on domestic core inflation - while CAD has no rates leg at all with both BoC core measures under target and WTI at $74.79.
symbols.risk: The oil sell-off is mature with a backwardated curve and light positioning, so a crude snapback on a failed Hormuz sign-off helps CAD immediately and the euro not at all.

symbols.why: REVERSED from RANGE. Both legs moved against the dollar in one session: June labour cash earnings at +3.4% restored the BoJ's wage-price precondition and put October back in play, while ADP at +44k and ISM services employment at 47.4 took the September Fed hike out of the price. Two-point score gap.
symbols.risk: A payroll beat tomorrow reverses the dollar leg instantly, and the MoF's own preference is for orderly moves rather than a fast rally - a violent yen appreciation is the one thing that would slow the official bid.

symbols.why: 99.84 at a seven-week low with three consecutive soft labour reads behind it, and the index's largest weight by far - EUR at 57.6% - is the strongest currency on the board. JPY at 13.6% has now flipped from neutral to supportive on the wage data.
symbols.risk: Tomorrow's payrolls is a two-way binary on this index specifically; a beat above +91k re-arms the September hike and clears 100 decisively.

symbols.why: REVERSED from RANGE. JPY is upgraded to STRENGTHENING on the June wage data - +3.4% headline, base pay accelerating to 3.4%, real wages positive for a sixth month - so the basket takes the directional long, the opposite ticket to the XXX/JPY shorts.
symbols.risk: The basket is the broadest yen expression, so it dilutes the strongest legs; a quiet BoJ September combined with a hot US payroll would stall it while individual crosses still work.

symbols.why: UPGRADED from RANGE. Two-point gap. Sterling has nothing domestic this week, but it does not need it - the dollar leg is doing the work after ADP at +44k and ISM services employment at 47.4, and cable is finally pressing the downward trendline near 1.3470 from below.
symbols.risk: This is a pure dollar-short expression with no British catalyst underneath, so a payroll beat unwinds it faster than it unwinds EUR/USD.

symbols.why: Two-point gap. The Aussie has the highest G10 policy rate, a live hawkish tail in the Q2 weighted median at 3.7% and a June trade balance that flipped to a AUD 1,929m surplus, against a dollar losing its hiking case on the labour data.
symbols.risk: Two binaries inside a week - US payrolls tomorrow and the RBA on Aug 11 where all four majors expect a hold. Terms of trade also slipped to 112 from 117.

symbols.why: UPGRADED from LOW-MED on the yen correction. Two-point gap restored: CAD has no rates leg with both core measures under target and crude at $74.79, against a yen whose wage-price cycle was just confirmed and whose central bank has October live again.
symbols.risk: Both legs can rally together - an oil snapback on a failed Hormuz sign-off rebuilds CAD at the same moment a quiet MoF lets the yen drift, and the Canadian jobs report lands tomorrow.

symbols.why: UPGRADED from LOW-MED. Two-point gap. Swiss July CPI at 0.4% with core 0.3%, under the SNB's own 0.7% forecast and pinned at zero to 2027, against a Japanese wage print that just restored the BoJ's tightening precondition.
symbols.risk: Both are haven currencies, so a failed Hormuz sign-off bids them together and the cross goes nowhere - and the franc would likely move first because its bid is organic rather than policy-driven.

symbols.why: Two-point gap. The 6-3 hawkish hold, 4.3% wage growth and a composite PMI at 52.1 give sterling a live rates story against a franc pinned at zero until 2027 with July CPI at 0.4% undershooting its own central bank's forecast.
symbols.risk: Sterling has no domestic catalyst this week, and a haven bid out of a failed Hormuz announcement lifts the franc leg regardless of the policy gap.

symbols.why: A 435bp nominal carry, the widest in the G10, with a Q2 weighted median rising to 3.7% and a June trade surplus of AUD 1,929m, against a franc at zero with core inflation stuck at 0.3% and a central bank that wants it lower.
symbols.risk: A dovish RBA on Aug 11 off the drop in inflation expectations to 4.7% would undercut the carry story, and a haven flare hits high-beta-versus-franc trades hardest.

symbols.why: Two-point gap and a 150bp policy gap still widening in direction - a BoE with three dissenters for a hike against a BoC with nothing to do and its only driver, crude, down roughly 13% in three sessions.
symbols.risk: Both legs are quiet domestically so this trades entirely off oil, and the Canadian employment report tomorrow is the one domestic event that can move the CAD leg on its own.

symbols.why: Two-point gap. A 210bp rate gap with a live hawkish tail at the RBA and a June trade surplus, against a BoC with core measures under target while the crude collapse lands squarely on the CAD leg.
symbols.risk: Both are commodity currencies exposed to the same global growth impulse, and an oil rebound helps CAD far more directly than the RBA could help AUD.

symbols.why: A record 26,202 after the crude collapse, strong corporate earnings and the AI technology rebound, now with the additional support of a Fed that has lost its hiking case - falling US real rates are a global equity tailwind and Brent is back under $79.
symbols.risk: The euro-area data that made the rally possible is the same data hardening the ECB's September hike, so a hawkish repricing plus an oil snapback is the double headwind, and the index is already at a record.

symbols.why: DOWNGRADED from MEDIUM. One-point gap now, not two. The euro still has the September hike, but the yen has stopped being a pure funding leg after June earnings at +3.4% and base pay accelerating to 3.4% restored the BoJ's precondition.
symbols.risk: This is the cross that suffers most from the yen upgrade being right - if October firms up, the score gap closes and a second joint MoF operation would hit it hard and without warning.

symbols.why: One-point gap. The euro has the harder catalyst - a September hike now backed by core inflation at 2.5% - while the RBA is a consensus hold with an argument rather than a decision behind it.
symbols.risk: The Aussie has its own hawkish tail in the Q2 weighted median at 3.7% and just posted a AUD 1,929m trade surplus, so this is a slow grind rather than a momentum trade.

symbols.why: One-point gap. Both committees are drifting hawkish, but only the ECB has an actual hike priced for September, and only the euro area printed accelerating core inflation and an upward PMI revision this week.
symbols.risk: The BoE's 6-3 vote with 4.3% wage growth means sterling's hawkish tail is real - this is the lowest-conviction of the euro longs and the one to drop first.

symbols.why: DOWNGRADED from MEDIUM. One-point gap now, not two. Unemployment at 5.6% still removes the only reason the kiwi was bid, but the dollar leg has deteriorated just as fast - ADP at +44k, ISM services employment at 47.4, DXY at 99.84.
symbols.risk: Both legs are weak, and a soft payroll tomorrow cushions the kiwi even on bad domestic news. New Zealand's July business confidence at 56.1 from 36.6 is the domestic counter.

symbols.why: One-point gap between two weak currencies. The RBNZ is finished hiking after a 5.6% unemployment print while the BoC was already on hold with both core measures under target - the kiwi has further to fall in expectation terms.
symbols.risk: The CAD leg is hostage to a crude market where the sell-off looks mature, so an oil bounce on the Hormuz announcement is the fastest way to lose this, and Canadian jobs land tomorrow.

symbols.why: One-point gap between two weakening currencies. The RBNZ has been stopped outright while the SNB has simply never started, so the direction of change favours the franc even though the level of carry does not.
symbols.risk: The franc is 250bp cheaper in carry terms and the SNB actively wants it weaker, so this pair pays nothing to hold - a thesis trade with negative carry, which caps how long to run it.

symbols.why: $74.79 after roughly 13% of downside in three sessions. The 60-day interim deal is drafted - inbound via an Iranian-controlled route, outbound through Omani waters, no transit fees - with Iranian sign-off reportedly completed and only the US blockade removal outstanding. But a deeply backwardated curve, tight Cushing stocks and light speculative positioning all warn the sell-off has run ahead of the physical market. The trade is made; do not press it.
symbols.risk: Two-way from here. Below $70 if the strait genuinely reopens and traffic flows as it briefly did in early July; a violent squeeze back above $84 if the sign-off slips again, which it has done repeatedly since Feb 28.

symbols.why: DOWNGRADED from LONG. Both legs now score -1 and both are weakening for opposite reasons - the dollar on three soft labour reads, the loonie on WTI at $74.79 with no rates leg. There is no score gap left to trade.
symbols.risk: Two employment reports land at the same minute tomorrow, one for each leg, which makes this the highest-variance range on the board - trade the levels, not the direction.

symbols.why: DOWNGRADED from LONG. Both legs score -1. The franc is unchanged and weak at zero to 2027 with July CPI at 0.4%, but the dollar leg has deteriorated faster on ADP, ISM services employment and DXY at a seven-week low.
symbols.risk: A soft payroll tomorrow hits the dollar leg while a failed Hormuz sign-off bids the franc leg - both sides can move together and cancel out.

symbols.why: Both currencies score -1 and both are weakening for unrelated reasons - CAD on the crude collapse, CHF on an inflation undershoot and a central bank that wants it lower. No edge either way.
symbols.risk: The two legs respond to opposite Hormuz outcomes: a real reopening lifts the franc relatively, a failed sign-off lifts CAD via oil - and either could land inside a week.

symbols.why: REVERSED from LONG. Both currencies now score +1 after the yen upgrade. A BoE with three dissenters against a BoJ whose wage precondition has just been met - two hawkish-drifting central banks with no gap to trade.
symbols.risk: This is the JPY cross most exposed to a second intervention because it is the highest-beta of the majors against the yen; if October firms up, this flips to a short rather than a range.

symbols.why: REVERSED from LONG. Both score +1. The Aussie has the trade surplus and the higher rate; the yen has the confirmed wage cycle and the official bid. Neither leg has an edge over the other this week.
symbols.risk: Two events inside a week point in opposite directions - the RBA on Aug 11 on one side, a possible second MoF operation and a live October BoJ on the other.

symbols.why: Both score +1. A BoE drifting hawkish with three dissenters against an RBA with a rising weighted median, a June trade surplus and a consensus hold - two similar stories with no score gap to trade.
symbols.risk: The RBA on Aug 11 is the only thing that separates them this week, and it cuts either way.

catalysts.event: Hormuz reopening — 60-day interim deal drafted, awaiting final sign-off
catalysts.note: The emerging arrangement is a 60-day interim deal under which ships enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through a southern route in Omani territorial waters, with no transit fees or tolls collected. Iranian and Omani negotiators have finalised the draft and, according to Trump administration accounts, Iran's leadership completed its approval process on Tuesday - though Iranian state television carried President Pezeshkian saying that interacting with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is very difficult at the moment. The outstanding condition is the removal of the US naval blockade, which Tehran has repeatedly named as a precondition. Trump said a deal could be announced as early as Wednesday and the US was aiming for a Wednesday announcement; it has not been confirmed. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began Feb 28, and WTI traded below $70 when traffic briefly flowed in early July. This is now a two-sided risk in crude, CAD, NZD, GER40 and the CHF block - and, via the inflation path, the single biggest input into the Fed's September decision after tomorrow's payrolls.

catalysts.event: Joint US-Japan FX intervention — now backed by a real rates story
catalysts.note: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama confirmed the MoF purchased yen in coordination with the US Treasury, the first joint operation since 2011, executed under the September 2025 Joint Statement and aimed at excessive volatility and disorderly movements, with both sides pledging not to hesitate to intervene again. The important change today is that the operation no longer stands alone: June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% y/y in line with consensus, base pay accelerated to 3.4% from 3.0%, and real wages rose 1.6% for a sixth straight month, so the level defence now sits on top of a genuine BoJ tightening case with October live. Size yen shorts for the possibility of a second operation; yen longs now have a fundamental leg as well as an administrative one.

Ordinarily a second-tier release, but it is the only labour data between the ISM services employment index at 47.4 and tomorrow's payrolls, and the market is now trading every hiring datapoint. A jump above 240k would effectively pre-confirm a weak payroll and extend the dollar break before the number lands.

The only Canadian input before tomorrow's employment report. With the BoC on a sixth hold and both core inflation measures under target, the loonie has no domestic story to trade, so this matters mainly as a check on whether the crude collapse is starting to show up in Canadian activity.

The biggest scheduled gate on the board and the only print that settles the dollar's direction. Consensus +91k after June's +57k, unemployment expected 4.3% from 4.2%, with April and May already revised down 74k combined. The bar has moved after ADP printed +44k against +70k expected and the ISM services employment index fell to 47.4 - a second sub-100k print now kills the September hike outright and confirms the dollar break; a clean beat re-arms it and turns every dollar-leg long on this board back into a range.

Lands at the same minute as US payrolls, which is exactly why it is worth trading through the crosses rather than USD/CAD. June delivered a +87.8k rebound and unemployment fell to 6.6%; a repeat would give the loonie its first non-oil argument in months and would put EUR/CAD, GBP/CAD and AUD/CAD at risk.

Last at 2.9% after edging down from 3.0%. The franc trades the haven bid and the SNB's zero rate rather than its labour market, so this only matters if it deteriorates enough to give the SNB a growth argument on top of a July CPI print at 0.4% that already undershoots its own Q3 forecast.

All four major Australian banks expect a hold at 4.35%, but the internals argue otherwise: the Q2 weighted median ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5%, services inflation to 4.0%, July services PMI was revised up to 53.6 with the composite at 53.2, and June trade swung to a AUD 1,929m surplus. Against that, consumer inflation expectations collapsed to 4.7% from 5.5%, terms of trade fell to 112 from 117 and cheaper crude will pull Q3 CPI down. The key event for AUD/NZD and AUD/CHF.

TE forecasts 3.4% headline after June's 3.5%, with core last at 2.6%. Energy drove more than 60% of a recent monthly gain, so whether the Hormuz premium actually comes out of crude feeds straight into this print. Note the tension: ISM services prices paid stayed at 70.3 even as the employment index collapsed to 47.4 - if inflation stays sticky while hiring stalls, the September FOMC becomes genuinely difficult rather than simply dovish.

Warsh's first Jackson Hole as Chair, and the venue where he would have to explain a September move after refusing to give guidance or submit a dot in July - a much harder speech to write now that ADP, JOLTS and the ISM services employment index have all rolled over. Runs Aug 27-28.

The hike is off. After Q2 unemployment printed 5.6% - the highest since Q3 2015 - with underutilisation at 13.8% and the labour cost index at 2.1%, the OCR stays at 2.50%. The interest is entirely in the language, and it is less one-sided than it looked: July business confidence jumped to 56.1 from 36.6 and the manufacturing PMI to 59.7, which gives the Bank room to retain a tightening bias even while acknowledging that the petrol-driven 4.1% Q2 CPI is unwinding.

A seventh consecutive hold at 2.25% is the base case with both core measures under target. The interest is whether the Bank acknowledges that cheaper crude removes the energy contribution holding headline CPI at 2.8%, which would open the door to a cut and take CAD lower still.

Roughly 70% of a hike is priced and, after July's HICP at 2.9% with core at 2.5%, Q2 GDP at +0.4% q/q and a final composite PMI revised up to 52.0, that pricing has a domestic foundation rather than depending on the oil premium Lagarde flagged. The counterargument is pipeline: producer prices decelerated to 4.6% from 5.9% and food inflation to 1.2%.

Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 with three dissents FOR a hike and no guidance or dot from Warsh. That case has been undermined in three sessions - JOLTS 7.14m, ADP +44k, ISM services employment 47.4 - while ISM manufacturing at 55.6 and services business activity at 59.1 say demand is fine. Hiring, not demand, is what has stopped. July jobs and July CPI both land first and will decide it.

TE forecasts a hold at 3.75%, but the Jul 30 vote was 6-3 against a 7-2 consensus and July services PMI swung back into expansion at 51.8 with the composite at 52.1. A fourth dissenter would confirm sterling's hawkish tail; the downwardly revised manufacturing PMI at 51.9 and a claimant count rising 6.7k are the counterarguments.

A hold at 1.00% remains the base case, but the October window is genuinely live again. June labour cash earnings rose 3.4% in line with consensus, base pay accelerated to 3.4% from 3.0%, real wages rose 1.6% for a sixth straight month and nominal growth has exceeded 3% for five months - the longest run in 34 years - which is the sustained wage-price cycle the Bank said it needed. Takata is already dissenting for 1.25% and Tamura wants a neutral rate near 2%. Tokyo July core CPI at 1.9% from 1.6% adds to it; the July Outlook Report's cut to FY2026 CPI of 2.5% is the offset.

A hold at 0% is universally expected, with panellists seeing no change until 2027 and July CPI at 0.4% undershooting the Bank's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast - Nomura now models Q3 at 0.5%. The relevance is language: the June statement pledged to lean against rapid franc APPRECIATION only, and any hardening of that is the main cap on EUR/CHF, GBP/CHF and AUD/CHF.

geopolitics: The Hormuz standoff has moved from negotiation to sign-off, and the shape of the deal is now public. It is an interim arrangement designed to run 60 days: inbound vessels enter the Persian Gulf via a route under Iranian control, outbound traffic exits through a southern corridor in Omani territorial waters, and neither side collects transit fees or tolls. Iranian and Omani negotiators have finalised the draft, and according to Trump administration accounts Iran's leadership completed its own approval process on Tuesday - although Iranian state television carried President Masoud Pezeshkian saying that interacting with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is very difficult at present, which is the kind of remark that has preceded every previous slippage. The outstanding condition is American: Tehran has consistently said the naval blockade must be lifted, and that is the concession the deal turns on. Trump said an announcement could come as early as Wednesday and the administration was aiming for exactly that; it has not landed. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's framing remains progress but not finality. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began on Feb 28, and when traffic briefly flowed in early July WTI traded below $70, which is the reference point for what a genuine reopening is worth. The market has now priced roughly 13% of it in three sessions, with WTI at $74.79 and Brent back under $79. The transmission into FX has shifted decisively today, and it is no longer primarily about the commodity currencies. It runs through the US inflation path: a reopening lowers the energy contribution to CPI, which lowers the Fed's hiking case, which lowers real rates - and that is why gold rose 3.8% to about $4,231, its largest daily gain since February, and silver 5.1% to $62.59, both RISING on de-escalation headlines that would ordinarily strip out a war premium. Falling real rates beat the disappearing risk premium, and that is the single most important read on this board. What remains directly exposed the old way is CAD, which has no rates leg with both BoC core measures under target, and NZD, whose Q2 CPI of 4.1% was 27.5% petrol. On crude itself the risk is genuinely two-sided: a deeply backwardated curve, tight Cushing stocks and light speculative positioning all warn that the paper market has run ahead of the physical one, and the announcement has slipped repeatedly since February - which is why USOIL stays RANGE rather than short.
